```{r}
#| label: setup
source("functions.R")
pop <- populations$die
```

# 1. What population are you sampling from?

A fair six sided die. Each face from 1 to 6 comes up with probability 1/6, so this is a discrete uniform distribution.
Its mean is 3.5 and its variance is 35/12 (SD about `r round(pop$sigma, 3)`). It is perfectly symmetric (skewness 0), and its
excess kurtosis is about `r round(pop$gamma2, 3)`: the tails are lighter than a normal distribution's, because no value
can be below 1 or above 6. It is also discrete: one roll can only be a whole number.

All three CLT assumptions hold here: each roll is independent of the others, every roll comes from the same die, and
the variance is finite. So the usual formula SE = sigma / sqrt(n) should apply.

The die is a different kind of test from the exponential. The exponential's problem was skewness, and the die
has none; its problems are flat, short tails and gaps between the possible values.

```{r}
#| label: population
#| fig.width: 7
#| fig.height: 4.5
set.seed(student_id)
popDraws <- pop$generator(100000)

share <- table(popDraws) / length(popDraws)
plot(1:6, as.numeric(share), type = "h", lwd = 8, col = "gray60", ylim = c(0, 0.32), xlim = c(-1, 8),
     main = "Die population: 100,000 rolls", xlab = "Face", ylab = "Proportion")
abline(h = 1 / 6, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
curve(dnorm(x, mean = pop$mu, sd = pop$sigma), add = TRUE, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("Simulated share", "True share 1/6", "Normal with same mean and SD"),
       col = c("gray60", "firebrick", "steelblue"), lwd = c(8, 2, 2), lty = c(1, 2, 1), bty = "n")

data.frame(
  quantity    = c("mean", "sd", "skewness", "excess kurtosis"),
  theoretical = c(pop$mu, pop$sigma, pop$gamma1, pop$gamma2),
  simulated   = c(mean(popDraws), sd(popDraws), skewness(popDraws), exKurtosis(popDraws))
)
```

Each face came up close to 1/6 of the time, and the simulated values are close to the theoretical ones. The normal
curve with the same mean and SD has `r round(100 * (1 - pnorm(6.5, pop$mu, pop$sigma) + pnorm(0.5, pop$mu, pop$sigma)), 1)` percent of its area outside 0.5 to 6.5 (half a step beyond the lowest and
highest faces), where the die has nothing, and it is highest in the middle while the die is flat. (The faces are 1 apart, so a share and a density
are on the same scale here, and the two can be drawn on one plot.)

## Does each face really approach 1/6?

Before checking the shares, I had a question. When people roll a real die a few times, the faces do not come up
1/6 of the time each. I wondered whether the share of each face really gets closer to 1/6 if I keep rolling.

There are two different reasons a share can differ from 1/6. The first is chance: with only a few rolls, some faces
come up more often just by luck. This should shrink as the number of rolls N grows (the law of large numbers), and
the standard error of a share, sqrt((1/6)(5/6) / N), says how fast: about 10 times smaller for every 100 times more
rolls. The second is a die that is not perfectly balanced. Real dice can be slightly biased: in Weldon's 1894
experiment (26,306 throws of 12 dice), fives and sixes came up 33.77 percent of the time instead of 33.33 percent,
which Pearson attributed to the hollowed out pips. More rolls do not remove this kind of bias; the shares then
approach the die's own probabilities, not 1/6. My simulation can only test the first reason, because
`sample(1:6, n, replace = TRUE)` gives every face probability exactly 1/6 by construction.

(Source: Z. Labby, "Weldon's Dice, Automated," CHANCE 22(4), 2009, pp. 6–13. I checked the 33.77 percent myself from the WeldonDice data in the R package vcd: about 0.3377 of the 12 × 26,306 dice showed a five or six.)

I tested this in two ways.

### One long sequence of rolls

First I followed the share of each face as the 100,000 rolls from my seed came in, and stopped to check it at N = 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000.

```{r}
#| label: runningShare
#| fig.width: 9
#| fig.height: 5
N <- 1:length(popDraws)
runShare <- sapply(1:6, function(f) cumsum(popDraws == f) / N)
showN <- unique(round(exp(seq(log(6), log(length(popDraws)), length.out = 400))))
plot(NULL, xlim = c(6, length(popDraws)), ylim = c(0, 0.65), log = "x", xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Number of rolls N (log scale)", ylab = "Share of the face so far",
     main = paste0("Share of each face as the rolls come in (seed ", student_id, ")"))
axis(1, at = c(10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000), labels = c("10", "100", "1,000", "10,000", "100,000"))
polygon(c(showN, rev(showN)),
        c(1 / 6 + 1.96 * sqrt((1 / 6) * (5 / 6) / showN), rev(1 / 6 - 1.96 * sqrt((1 / 6) * (5 / 6) / showN))),
        col = "gray90", border = NA)
faceCols <- c("black", "steelblue", "darkorange", "darkgreen", "purple", "firebrick")
for (f in 1:6) lines(showN, runShare[showN, f], col = faceCols[f], lwd = 1.5)
abline(h = 1 / 6, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c(paste("face", 1:6), "1/6 +/- 1.96 SE"), col = c(faceCols, "gray80"),
       lwd = c(rep(1.5, 6), NA), pch = c(rep(NA, 6), 15), pt.cex = 2, bty = "n", ncol = 2, cex = 0.85)

checkN <- c(10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000)
runTable <- data.frame(
  rolls = format(checkN, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE),
  round(runShare[checkN, ], 3),
  largestGap = sapply(checkN, function(k) max(abs(runShare[k, ] - 1 / 6)))
)
names(runTable)[2:7] <- paste("face", 1:6)
knitr::kable(runTable, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

After 10 rolls the shares were far from 1/6 (face `r which.max(runShare[10, ])` came up `r round(max(runShare[10, ]) * 10)` times out of 10, and face `r paste(which(runShare[10, ] == 0), collapse = " and ")` not at all), which is
what I see when I roll a die by hand. As the rolls came in, every face moved toward 1/6, and the gray band, which shrinks like 1 / sqrt(N), shows how close chance alone should bring them. After 100,000 rolls the largest gap was `r format(round(runTable$largestGap[checkN == 100000], 4), scientific = FALSE)`.

### How large does N need to be?

One sequence is only one example; a different sequence of rolls would wander differently. To see how accurate the law of large numbers is at each N, I repeated the whole experiment `r format(1000, big.mark = ",")` times for each N (resetting the seed
before each N, as in the rest of my analysis) and recorded the largest gap from 1/6 among the six faces each time.

Before running it, I used the standard error to predict. For one face, 95 percent of the shares should be within 1.96 × sqrt((1/6)(5/6) / N) of 1/6. Setting that equal to a tolerance d and solving for N gives N = 1.96² × (5/36) / d². For d = 0.01 (one percentage point) that is about `r format(ceiling(1.96^2 * (5 / 36) / 0.01^2), big.mark = ",")` rolls, and for d = 0.001 it is about `r format(ceiling(1.96^2 * (5 / 36) / 0.001^2), big.mark = ",")` rolls. Since all six faces have to be close at the same time, I expected to need somewhat more than that.

```{r}
#| label: lawOfLargeNumbers
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 4.5
lawN <- c(10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000)
lawReps <- 1000
lawTable <- do.call(rbind, lapply(lawN, function(k) {
  set.seed(student_id)
  gaps <- replicate(lawReps, {
    shares <- tabulate(pop$generator(k), nbins = 6) / k
    max(abs(shares - 1 / 6))
  })
  data.frame(rolls = k,
             typicalGap = median(gaps),
             gap95 = unname(quantile(gaps, 0.95)),
             withinOnePoint = mean(gaps <= 0.01),
             withinTenthPoint = mean(gaps <= 0.001))
}))
knitr::kable(transform(lawTable, rolls = format(rolls, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)),
             digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)

plot(lawTable$rolls, lawTable$typicalGap, log = "xy", pch = 16, cex = 1.4, xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Number of rolls N (log scale)", ylab = "Typical largest gap from 1/6 (log scale)",
     main = "How fast the shares approach 1/6")
axis(1, at = lawN, labels = format(lawN, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE))
lines(lawN, lawTable$typicalGap[1] * sqrt(lawN[1] / lawN), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Simulated (median of 1,000 repeats)", "Shrinking like 1 / sqrt(N)"),
       col = c("black", "firebrick"), pch = c(16, NA), lty = c(NA, 2), lwd = c(NA, 2), bty = "n")
shrink <- lawTable$typicalGap[-length(lawN)] / lawTable$typicalGap[-1]
```

`typicalGap` is the median of the largest gap over the `r format(lawReps, big.mark = ",")` repeats, and `gap95` is the gap that 95 percent of the repeats stayed under. `withinOnePoint` and `withinTenthPoint` are the shares of repeats in which all six faces were within 0.01 and within 0.001 of 1/6.

* The gap keeps shrinking: every time N grew 10 times, the typical gap became `r round(min(shrink), 1)` to `r round(max(shrink), 1)` times smaller, close to sqrt(10) = `r round(sqrt(10), 2)`. The points follow the red 1 / sqrt(N) line.
* With 10 rolls, being within one percentage point is impossible: each share must be a multiple of 1/10, and the
  closest one to 1/6 is 0.2, which is 0.033 away. So "close to 1/6" also needs enough rolls for the share to be able to land near 1/6, the same gap problem I found for the sample mean later in this file.
* All six faces were within one percentage point in `r round(100 * lawTable$withinOnePoint[lawN == 1000])` percent of the repeats with 1,000 rolls and
  `r round(100 * lawTable$withinOnePoint[lawN == 10000])` percent with 10,000 rolls, which fits the prediction of about `r format(ceiling(1.96^2 * (5 / 36) / 0.01^2), big.mark = ",")` rolls for one face.
* Within 0.001 is much harder: even with 100,000 rolls it happened in only `r round(100 * lawTable$withinTenthPoint[lawN == 100000], 1)` percent of the repeats, because it needs about `r format(ceiling(1.96^2 * (5 / 36) / 0.001^2), big.mark = ",")` rolls for a single face.

So the shares do approach 1/6, but there is no N where they "arrive". The law of large numbers says the gap goes to 0 as N grows; how large N must be depends on how close I need to be, and each extra digit of accuracy costs 100 times more rolls. This is the same 1 / sqrt(N) rate that appears in the CLT formula sigma / sqrt(n).

## Is each face really 1/6?

The shares above are close to 1/6, but "close" needs a scale. With 100,000 rolls, the share of one face should
be 1/6 give or take about sqrt((1/6)(5/6) / 100,000) = `r round(sqrt((1/6) * (5/6) / 100000), 5)` (one standard error), just from chance. So for
each face I measured how far its share was from 1/6 in standard errors, and I ran a chi square test that checks
all six faces at once.

```{r}
#| label: faceCheck
#| fig.width: 7
#| fig.height: 4.5
rollSE <- sqrt((1 / 6) * (5 / 6) / 100000)
faceCheck <- data.frame(
  face = 1:6,
  share = as.numeric(share),
  gapInSE = (as.numeric(share) - 1 / 6) / rollSE
)
knitr::kable(faceCheck, digits = 4)
faceTest <- chisq.test(table(popDraws), p = rep(1 / 6, 6))
faceTest

plot(1:6, faceCheck$share, pch = 16, cex = 1.4, ylim = 1 / 6 + c(-4, 4) * rollSE,
     xlab = "Face", ylab = "Share of 100,000 rolls", main = paste("Share of each face with seed", student_id))
rect(0.5, 1 / 6 - 1.96 * rollSE, 6.5, 1 / 6 + 1.96 * rollSE, col = "gray90", border = NA)
abline(h = 1 / 6, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
points(1:6, faceCheck$share, pch = 16, cex = 1.4)
legend("topright", c("Share of the face", "1/6", "1/6 +/- 1.96 SE"),
       col = c("black", "firebrick", "gray80"), pch = c(16, NA, 15), lty = c(NA, 2, NA),
       lwd = c(NA, 2, NA), pt.cex = c(1.4, NA, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

All six shares are inside the gray band (1/6 ± 1.96 standard errors); the largest gap was
`r round(max(abs(faceCheck$gapInSE)), 2)` standard errors. The chi square test did not reject a fair die (p = `r round(faceTest$p.value, 3)`).
So the 100,000 rolls from my seed behave like a fair die, and the small differences from 1/6 are the size
chance alone would produce.

# 2. What did you expect before running the simulation?

I made five predictions before running anything.

Center and spread: the mean of the sample means should be 3.5 and their SD should be sigma / sqrt(n) at every n,
including n = 1, for the same reason as in the other files (only independence and a finite variance are needed).

Skewness: the die is symmetric, so the sample mean is symmetric too, and its skewness should be 0 at every n
(gamma1 / sqrt(n) = 0). The skewness check should never be the one that decides.

Kurtosis: the excess kurtosis of the mean should be gamma2 / n = `r round(pop$gamma2, 3)` / n. It is negative, so the
sampling distribution should start out too flat with short tails, and then fill in toward the normal shape.
My kurtosis cutoff is `r criteria$kurt`, so I need `r round(abs(pop$gamma2), 3)` / n ≤ `r criteria$kurt`, which means

```{r}
#| label: prediction
kurtN <- ceiling(abs(pop$gamma2) / criteria$kurt)
kurtN
data.frame(n = c(1, 2, 5, 30),
           predSkew = pop$gamma1 / sqrt(c(1, 2, 5, 30)),
           predKurt = pop$gamma2 / c(1, 2, 5, 30))
```

So from the formulas alone, kurtosis decides, at about n = `r kurtN`, which is much faster than the exponential.

Tails: one roll is at most 2.5 away from 3.5, which is only `r round(2.5 / pop$sigma, 2)` SDs. So at n = 1 no value can be beyond
±1.96 SDs, and I expected the tail shares to be 0 instead of 2.5 percent.

Discreteness: the mean of n rolls is a sum of whole numbers divided by n, so it can only take values in steps of
1 / n, between 1 and 6. That is 5n + 1 possible values (6 at n = 1, 11 at n = 2, 26 at n = 5).

## What the formulas cannot see

The skewness and kurtosis formulas only give two numbers. To see what those two numbers miss, I did not need a
simulation: for a die, the exact distribution of the mean can be counted. The sum of n rolls is the sum of n − 1 rolls
plus one more roll, so I built the probabilities one roll at a time.

```{r}
#| label: exactDie
exactDieMean <- function(n) {
  p <- rep(1 / 6, 6)
  if (n > 1) {
    for (i in 2:n) {
      new <- rep(0, length(p) + 5)
      for (face in 1:6) {
        idx <- face:(face + length(p) - 1)
        new[idx] <- new[idx] + p / 6
      }
      p <- new
    }
  }
  data.frame(value = (n:(6 * n)) / n, prob = p)
}

largestCdfGap <- function(e, n, shift = 0) {
  F <- cumsum(e$prob)
  Fbefore <- c(0, head(F, -1))
  normalF <- pnorm(e$value + shift, mean = pop$mu, sd = pop$sigma / sqrt(n))
  if (shift == 0) max(abs(F - normalF), abs(Fbefore - normalF)) else max(abs(F - normalF))
}

exactN <- c(1, 2, 5, 8, 30, 100)
exactTable <- do.call(rbind, lapply(exactN, function(n) {
  e <- exactDieMean(n)
  d <- e$value - sum(e$value * e$prob)
  v <- sum(d^2 * e$prob)
  data.frame(n = n,
             possibleValues = nrow(e),
             stepInSE = (1 / n) / (pop$sigma / sqrt(n)),
             formulaKurt = pop$gamma2 / n,
             exactKurt = sum(d^4 * e$prob) / v^2 - 3,
             exactSkew = sum(d^3 * e$prob) / v^1.5,
             largestCdfGap = largestCdfGap(e, n))
}))
knitr::kable(exactTable, digits = 4)
```

`exactKurt` and `exactSkew` come from the counted probabilities, with no random numbers. They agree with the formulas
to every digit shown, so the formulas are not wrong. What they cannot see is the last two columns. `stepInSE` is the
gap between two neighbouring possible values, measured in standard errors, and `largestCdfGap` is the largest vertical
distance between the exact CDF of the mean (a staircase) and the normal CDF. At n = 8 that distance is
`r round(100 * exactTable$largestCdfGap[exactTable$n == 8], 2)` percentage points, even though the kurtosis there is only `r round(exactTable$formulaKurt[exactTable$n == 8], 3)`.

```{r}
#| label: formulaBlind
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 4
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (n in c(2, 8)) {
  e <- exactDieMean(n)
  se <- pop$sigma / sqrt(n)
  plot(stepfun(e$value, c(0, cumsum(e$prob))), do.points = FALSE, lwd = 2,
       xlim = pop$mu + c(-3, 3) * se, main = paste("Exact CDF of the mean, n =", n),
       xlab = "Sample mean", ylab = "P(mean <= x)")
  curve(pnorm(x, mean = pop$mu, sd = se), add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
}
nLine <- exp(seq(log(1), log(100), length.out = 400))
plot(nLine, 1 / nLine, type = "l", log = "x", lwd = 2, col = "darkorange", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Sample size n (log scale)", ylab = "Size relative to n = 1",
     main = "Kurtosis shrinks faster than the steps")
lines(nLine, 1 / sqrt(nLine), lwd = 2, col = "black")
abline(v = kurtN, lty = 3, col = "gray40")
legend("topright", c("Kurtosis: 1 / n", "Step in SE units: 1 / sqrt(n)"),
       col = c("darkorange", "black"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
par(old)
```

The two left panels show the exact CDF (black staircase) against the normal CDF (red). At n = 2 the steps are large;
at n = 8 they are smaller but still clearly there. The right panel shows why the steps outlast the kurtosis: the
kurtosis formula shrinks like 1 / n, but the step in SE units is (1 / n) / (sigma / sqrt(n)) = 1 / (sigma × sqrt(n)), which
only shrinks like 1 / sqrt(n). At n = `r kurtN`, where my kurtosis cutoff is first met, the kurtosis is down to
`r round(100 / kurtN)` percent of its n = 1 value but the step is still `r round(100 / sqrt(kurtN))` percent.

So I expected the gaps to show up in the QQ check, because a QQ plot of a variable with gaps is a staircase, and that
they might keep the QQ check failing after kurtosis passes. I could not predict for how long, because there is no
formula that turns the step size into my QQ correlation.

# 3. Which sample sizes did you investigate?

## Coarse grid, then a finer grid

I expected a fast answer (near n = `r kurtN`), so my coarse grid is dense at small n: `r paste(pop$coarse, collapse = ", ")`.
As in the other files, the code then adds values between the last failing n and the first passing n.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
res <- analyzePopulation(pop)
tab <- res$table
nStar <- smallestN(tab)
added <- setdiff(tab$n, pop$coarse)
showTable(tab)
```

The finer grid added `r paste(added, collapse = ", ")`, the only whole number between the last failing and the first passing
coarse value.

Number of distinct values the sample mean took in my simulation:

```{r}
#| label: distinct
distinct <- data.frame(
  n = tab$n,
  possible = 5 * tab$n + 1,
  observed = sapply(res$means, function(m) length(unique(m)))
)
knitr::kable(distinct, row.names = FALSE)
allSeen <- max(distinct$n[distinct$possible == distinct$observed])
```

Up to n = `r allSeen` every possible value showed up. For large n the extreme values (all ones or all sixes) are so rare that
they never appeared in `r format(num, big.mark = ",")` repetitions.

## Which check failed?

```{r}
#| label: whichFailed
failTable <- data.frame(
  n = tab$n,
  skewOK = abs(tab$skew) <= criteria$skew,
  kurtOK = abs(tab$exKurt) <= criteria$kurt,
  qqOK = tab$qqCor >= criteria$qqCor
)
knitr::kable(failTable)
kurtPass <- min(tab$n[failTable$kurtOK & failTable$skewOK])
```

The skewness check passed at every n, as expected. The kurtosis check passed from n = `r kurtPass` (my prediction
was `r kurtN`). But the QQ check kept failing after that, so the QQ check, not kurtosis, decided the answer.

## Is it the gaps or the short tails?

The QQ correlation of the die means could be low for two reasons: the gaps between possible values (discreteness),
or the short tails (negative kurtosis). To separate them I ran two extra versions with the same seed:

* Die with the gaps filled in: I added a small uniform random amount between −1 / (2n) and 1 / (2n) to each sample
  mean. This spreads every spike evenly over its own step, so the gaps disappear and the shape stays almost the same.
* Continuous uniform population from 0.5 to 6.5: same mean as the die and almost the same kurtosis (−1.2), but no gaps.
  Its SD is a little larger (`r round(sqrt(3), 3)` instead of `r round(pop$sigma, 3)`), which does not matter here because the QQ correlation does
  not depend on the scale.

```{r}
#| label: gapsOrTails
gapN <- c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30)
uniformGen <- function(n) runif(n, min = 0.5, max = 6.5)
gapsOrTails <- do.call(rbind, lapply(gapN, function(n) {
  set.seed(student_id)
  dieMeans <- simMeans(pop$generator, n)
  filled <- dieMeans + runif(num, -1 / (2 * n), 1 / (2 * n))
  set.seed(student_id)
  uniMeans <- simMeans(uniformGen, n)
  data.frame(n = n,
             qqDie = qqCorrelation(dieMeans),
             qqDieFilled = qqCorrelation(filled),
             qqUniform = qqCorrelation(uniMeans),
             kurtDie = exKurtosis(dieMeans),
             kurtUniform = exKurtosis(uniMeans))
}))
knitr::kable(gapsOrTails, digits = 4)
filledPass <- min(gapN[gapsOrTails$qqDieFilled >= criteria$qqCor])
```

Filling in the gaps raised the QQ correlation to almost the same value as the continuous uniform, at every n, and it
passed my cutoff from n = `r filledPass`. The kurtosis of the die and the uniform are also close. So the short tails are not
the problem: almost all of the gap between the die and a straight QQ line comes from discreteness.

## Choosing my QQ cutoff again

Because the QQ check decides here, I checked how much the answer depends on the QQ cutoff, keeping the other
cutoffs the same.

```{r}
#| label: qqCompare
qqValues <- c(0.995, 0.998, 0.999)
qqCompare <- data.frame(
  qqCut = qqValues,
  chosenN = sapply(qqValues, function(q) {
    crit <- criteria
    crit$qqCor <- q
    smallestN(tab, crit)
  })
)
knitr::kable(qqCompare)
```

On the die the QQ cutoff moves the answer a lot, from `r qqCompare$chosenN[1]` to `r qqCompare$chosenN[3]`. With 0.995 the answer equals
the kurtosis answer, so the gaps do not change it. With 0.998 and 0.999 the gaps decide. I kept 0.998 so that all
populations are judged by the same standard; I chose 0.998 in 01normal.qmd and checked it on the exponential in 03exponential.qmd.

# 4. When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal?

$$\boxed{n = `r nStar`}$$

```{r}
#| label: summaryNumbers
star     <- tab[tab$n == nStar, ]
lastFail <- tab[tab$n == max(tab$n[tab$n < nStar & !tab$normalEnough]), ]
failed   <- c(skewness = abs(lastFail$skew) > criteria$skew,
              kurtosis = abs(lastFail$exKurt) > criteria$kurt,
              QQ = lastFail$qqCor < criteria$qqCor)
at1      <- tab[tab$n == 1, ]
at30     <- tab[tab$n == 30, ]
seRange  <- range(tab$seRatio)
meanGapZ <- abs(tab$simMean - tab$theoMean) / (tab$theoSE / sqrt(num))
```

My prediction from kurtosis was n = `r kurtN`, and the simulation gave n = `r nStar`. The QQ check decided, so the plot below
shows the QQ correlation for the die, the die with the gaps filled in, and the continuous uniform.

```{r}
#| label: whyN
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig.height: 5.5
plot(NULL, xlim = range(gapN), ylim = c(0.985, 1), log = "x",
     xlab = "Sample size n (log scale)", ylab = "QQ correlation",
     main = paste0("Why n = ", nStar, ": the gaps keep the QQ correlation low"))
lines(gapsOrTails$n, gapsOrTails$qqUniform, col = "gray50", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
lines(gapsOrTails$n, gapsOrTails$qqDieFilled, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, type = "o", pch = 16)
lines(gapsOrTails$n, gapsOrTails$qqDie, col = "black", lwd = 2, type = "o", pch = 16)
abline(h = criteria$qqCor, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = nStar, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, lty = 3)
abline(v = kurtN, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2, lty = 3)
legend("bottomright",
       c("Die", "Die with gaps filled in", "Continuous uniform", paste("Cutoff", criteria$qqCor),
         paste("Kurtosis prediction n =", kurtN), paste("Chosen n =", nStar)),
       col = c("black", "steelblue", "gray50", "firebrick", "darkorange", "steelblue"),
       lty = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3), lwd = 2, pch = c(16, 16, NA, NA, NA, NA), bty = "n")
```

How to read it: the blue and gray lines (no gaps) cross my cutoff early. The black line (the real die) sits below them
at every n and only reaches the cutoff at n = `r nStar`. The distance between the black and blue lines is the cost of
discreteness, and it shrinks as n grows because the steps of 1 / n get smaller.

# 5. How do the simulated mean and standard error compare with theory?

```{r}
#| label: seCheck
tab[, c("n", "simMean", "theoMean", "simSD", "theoSE", "seRatio", "seOK")]
```

```{r}
#| label: sePlot
plotSE(tab, label = "Die")
```

Center: the simulated mean was within 2 Monte Carlo standard errors (theoretical SE / sqrt(num)) of 3.5 at
`r sum(meanGapZ <= 2)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes, with a largest gap of `r round(max(meanGapZ), 2)`.

Spread: the SE ratio stayed between `r round(seRange[1], 3)` and `r round(seRange[2], 3)`, and `r sum(tab$seOK)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes passed my
5 percent SE check, including n = 1. The ratio was below 1 at `r sum(tab$seRatio[tab$n >= 15] < 1)` of the `r sum(tab$n >= 15)` sample sizes from n = 15 on. As in
03exponential.qmd, these rows share one random stream, so they move together and are not independent checks.

# 6. Why did you choose that value?

With default breaks, a histogram of a discrete variable can be misleading: a bin can land between two possible values
and stay empty, or hold two of them. So for the die I set the breaks halfway between the possible values of the mean,
which are 1 / n apart. Each bar then holds exactly one possible value. The red curve is the normal density with mean 3.5
and SD sigma / sqrt(n).

```{r}
#| label: samplingPlots
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 6
plotLattice(res, nShow = unique(c(1, 2, nStar, 30)), mu = pop$mu, theoSE = iidSE(pop$sigma), label = pop$label)
```

At n = 1 the histogram is six bars of equal height and the QQ plot is six flat steps. At n = 2 the bars already form a
triangle (the sum of two dice), and the QQ plot is a staircase that roughly follows the line, with long flat steps at
both ends. At n = `r nStar` the bars follow the red curve closely, and the QQ plot follows the line with small steps. At n = 30
the steps are hard to see.

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 4
plotConvergence(tab, label = "Die")
```

The skewness stays near 0 at every n, and the kurtosis rises toward 0 along the red prediction `r round(pop$gamma2, 3)` / n.

Tails: at n = 1 the lower and upper tail shares beyond ±1.96 were `r round(100 * at1$tailLow, 2)` and `r round(100 * at1$tailHigh, 2)` percent, as
predicted. At n = 30 they were `r round(100 * at30$tailLow, 2)` and `r round(100 * at30$tailHigh, 2)` percent, close to 2.5. So for the die, n = 30 is more than
enough under my standard; the rule of thumb is conservative here, the opposite of the exponential.

I chose n = `r nStar` because:

* At n = `r nStar` the skewness was `r round(star$skew, 3)`, the excess kurtosis `r round(star$exKurt, 3)` and the QQ correlation
  `r round(star$qqCor, 4)`, all within my cutoffs, and every larger n I tested also passed.
* At the largest n that still failed (n = `r lastFail$n`), the check that failed was `r paste(names(failed)[failed], collapse = " and ")`
  (QQ correlation `r round(lastFail$qqCor, 4)`).
* The gaps or tails experiment showed that the QQ failures at n = `r kurtPass` to `r lastFail$n` come from discreteness, not from
  the shape.

# 7. What surprised you?

```{r}
#| label: predictionCheck
predictionCheck <- data.frame(
  Prediction = c(
    "Mean of the sample means equals 3.5 at every n (within noise)",
    "SE equals sigma / sqrt(n) at every n, including n = 1",
    "Skewness near 0 at every n; skewness never decides",
    paste0("Kurtosis about ", round(pop$gamma2, 3), " / n; passes at about n = ", kurtN),
    "From the formulas: kurtosis decides the answer",
    paste("From the formulas: smallest normal n is about", kurtN),
    "Tail shares 0 at n = 1",
    "Shapiro Wilk rejects at almost every n"
  ),
  Result = c(
    paste0("Within 2 Monte Carlo SEs at ", sum(meanGapZ <= 2), " of ", nrow(tab), " n"),
    paste0("SE ratio ", round(seRange[1], 3), " to ", round(seRange[2], 3), "; ", sum(tab$seOK), " of ", nrow(tab), " passed"),
    paste0("Largest |skewness| ", round(max(abs(tab$skew)), 3)),
    paste("Kurtosis passed from n =", kurtPass),
    paste0("Last failure (n = ", lastFail$n, ") failed on ", paste(names(failed)[failed], collapse = " and ")),
    paste("n =", nStar),
    paste0(round(100 * at1$tailLow, 2), "% and ", round(100 * at1$tailHigh, 2), "%"),
    paste0("Rejected at ", sum(tab$swP < 0.05), " of ", nrow(tab), " n")
  ),
  Match = c(ifelse(all(meanGapZ <= 2), "Same", "Different"), "Same", "Same", "Same",
            "Different", "Different", "Same", "Same")
)
knitr::kable(predictionCheck)
```

The formulas worked: skewness stayed near 0, and kurtosis followed `r round(pop$gamma2, 3)` / n and passed at n = `r kurtPass`.
What I got wrong was which check would decide. From the formulas I expected kurtosis, but the QQ check still failed at
n = `r kurtPass` to `r lastFail$n`, where kurtosis had already passed. Section 2 had warned me that the steps shrink more slowly
than the kurtosis, and the gaps or tails experiment in section 3 confirmed that the steps were the reason. The
skewness and kurtosis formulas do not know about discreteness at all, so the formula prediction was too optimistic here.

This made me think about what "normal enough" means for a discrete variable. A sample mean of dice can never be exactly
normal, at any n, because it always has gaps. My QQ check measures shape and discreteness together. For a question like
"what is the chance that the average of 8 rolls is above 4?", the gaps matter: an average of exactly 4 has probability
`r round(100 * exactDieMean(8)$prob[abs(exactDieMean(8)$value - 4) < 1e-9], 2)` percent, so P(mean > 4) and P(mean ≥ 4) differ by that much. So I think it is reasonable that my
standard counts the gaps.

I also checked how much of the CDF gap from section 2 is only about the steps. If I evaluate the normal CDF half a
step to the right of each possible value (a continuity correction), the largest gap at n = 8 drops from
`r round(100 * exactTable$largestCdfGap[exactTable$n == 8], 2)` to `r round(100 * largestCdfGap(exactDieMean(8), 8, shift = 1 / 16), 2)` percentage points. So the normal curve describes the die mean well at n = 8; the error
without the correction comes almost entirely from where the steps are.

Compared with the exponential (n = 100), the die needed far fewer rolls, even though its population looks nothing like a
normal curve. In my two non normal populations so far, the skewed one converged slowly and the symmetric one fast.

## Limitations

* My answer of n = `r nStar` depends on the QQ cutoff: `r qqCompare$chosenN[1]` with 0.995 and `r qqCompare$chosenN[3]` with 0.999. On the die
  the QQ cutoff mostly decides how much discreteness I accept.
* At n = `r nStar` the QQ correlation was `r round(star$qqCor, 5)`, only `r format(round(star$qqCor - criteria$qqCor, 5), scientific = FALSE)` above my cutoff. A different seed
  could put it just below, and the answer would move to the next n.
* My QQ check judges the normal approximation without a continuity correction. Section 7 showed that with one, the
  CDF gap at n = 8 is only `r round(100 * largestCdfGap(exactDieMean(8), 8, shift = 1 / 16), 2)` percentage points, so for probability
  calculations with a correction, a smaller n than `r nStar` might already be good enough.
* The QQ correlation is a summary of the whole distribution. It does not show where the steps are; the QQ plots in
  section 6 do.
* All rows come from one random stream (seed `r student_id`), so they are not independent of each other.
